'''William Whiston''' (9 December 1667{{snd}}22 August 1752) was an English [[theologian]], historian, [[Natural philosophy|natural philosopher]], and [[mathematician]], a leading figure in the popularisation of the ideas of [[Isaac Newton]]. He is now probably best known for helping to instigate the [[Longitude Act]] in 1714 (and his attempts to win [[longitude prize|the rewards]] that it promised) and his important translations of the ''[[Antiquities of the Jews]]'' and other works by [[Josephus]] (which are still in print).  He was a prominent exponent of [[Arianism]] and wrote ''[[A New Theory of the Earth]]''.

Whiston succeeded his mentor Newton as [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]. In 1710 he lost the professorship and was expelled from the university as a result of his unorthodox religious views. Whiston rejected the notion of eternal torment in hellfire, which he viewed as absurd, cruel, and an insult to God. What especially pitted him against church authorities was his denial of the doctrine of the [[Trinity]], which he believed had [[Paganism|pagan]] origins.

==Early life and career==
Whiston was born to Josiah Whiston (1622–1685) and Katherine Rosse (1639–1701) at [[Norton Juxta Twycross|Norton-juxta-Twycross]], in [[Leicestershire]], where his father was [[Rector (ecclesiastical)|rector]].  His mother was daughter of the previous rector at Norton-juxta-Twycross, Gabriel Rosse.  Josiah Whiston was a [[Presbyterianism|presbyterian]], but retained his rectorship after the [[Stuart Restoration]] in 1660.  William Whiston was educated privately, for his health, and so that he could act as [[amanuensis]] to his blind father.<ref name="ODNB Whiston">{{Cite ODNB|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/29217|title=Whiston, William}}</ref><ref name="EB1911">{{EB1911|inline=1 |wstitle=Whiston, William |volume=28 |page=597}}</ref> He studied at [[Queen Elizabeth's Mercian School|Queen Elizabeth Grammar School]] at [[Tamworth, Staffordshire]]. After his father's death, he entered [[Clare College, Cambridge]] as a [[sizar]] in 1686. He applied himself to mathematical study, was awarded the degree of Bachelor of Arts (BA) (1690), and AM (1693), and was elected Fellow in 1691 and probationary senior Fellow in 1693.<ref name="ODNB Whiston"/><ref>{{acad|id=WHSN686W|name=Whiston, William}}</ref>

[[William Lloyd (bishop of Worcester)|William Lloyd]] ordained Whiston at [[Lichfield]] in 1693. In 1694, claiming ill health, he resigned his tutorship at Clare to [[Richard Laughton]], chaplain to [[John Moore (Bishop of Norwich)|John Moore]], the [[bishop of Norwich]], and swapped positions with him. He now divided his time between Norwich, Cambridge and London. In 1698 Moore gave him the living of [[Lowestoft]] where he became rector. In 1699 he resigned his Fellowship of Clare College and left to marry.<ref name="ODNB Whiston"/>

Whiston first met [[Isaac Newton]] in 1694 and attended some of his lectures, though he first found them, by his own admission, incomprehensible.  Encouraged after reading a paper by [[David Gregory (mathematician)|David Gregory]] on [[Newtonianism|Newtonian philosophy]], he set out to master Newton's ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Principia mathematica]]'' thereafter.  He and Newton became friends.<ref name="ODNB Whiston"/> In 1701 Whiston resigned his living to become Isaac Newton's substitute, giving the Lucasian lectures at Cambridge.<ref name="EB1911"/> He succeeded Newton as Lucasian professor in 1702. There followed a period of joint research with [[Roger Cotes]], appointed with Whiston's patronage to the [[Plumian professorship]] in 1706. Students at the Cotes–Whiston experimental philosophy course included [[Stephen Hales]], [[William Stukeley]], and [[Joseph Wasse]].{{sfn|Knox|2003|p=145}}

==Newtonian theologian==

In 1707 Whiston was [[Boyle lecturer]]; this lecture series was at the period a significant opportunity for Newton's followers, including [[Richard Bentley]] and [[Samuel Clarke]], to express their views, especially in opposition to the rise of [[deism]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Shank |first=J. B. |title=The Newton Wars and the Beginning of the French Enlightenment|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BBusxgu8-AAC&pg=PA128|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2008|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-74947-1|pages=128–29}}</ref> The "Newtonian" line came to include, with Bentley, Clarke and Whiston in particular, a defence of [[natural law]] by returning to the definition of [[Augustine of Hippo]] of a [[miracle]] (a cause of human wonderment), rather than the prevailing concept of a divine intervention against nature, which went back to [[Anselm of Canterbury|Anselm]]. This move was intended to undermine arguments of deists and sceptics.<ref>{{cite book |last=Shaw |first=Jane |title=Miracles in Enlightenment England|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4_UXe_Cat7wC&pg=PA31|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2006|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=978-0-300-11272-6|pages=31, 171}}</ref> The Boyle lectures dwelt on the connections between biblical prophecies, dramatic physical events such as floods and eclipses, and their explanations in terms of science.<ref>{{ThoemmesBritish17C|Whiston, William|875}}</ref> On the other hand, Whiston was alive to possible connections of prophecy with current affairs: the [[War of the Spanish Succession]], and later the [[Jacobite rebellions]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=Sara Schechner|author2=Sara Schechner Genuth|title=Comets, popular culture, and the birth of modern cosmology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_U3rRP-P684C&pg=PA292|access-date=23 May 2013|year=1999|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-00925-4|page=292}}</ref>

Whiston supported a qualified [[biblical literalism]]: the literal meaning should be the default, unless there was a good reason to think otherwise.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kidd |first=Colin |title=British Identities before Nationalism|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I2EIlJISeUMC&pg=PA45|access-date=22 May 2013|year=1999|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-42572-8|page=45}}</ref> This view again went back to Augustine. Newton's attitude to the [[cosmogony]] of [[Thomas Burnet (theologian)|Thomas Burnet]] reflected on the language of the [[Genesis creation narrative]]; as did Whiston's alternative cosmogony. Moses as author of ''Genesis'' was not necessarily writing as a natural philosopher, nor as a law-giver, but for a particular audience.{{sfn|Poole|2010|p=68}} The new cosmogonies of Burnet, Whiston and [[John Woodward (naturalist)|John Woodward]] were all criticised for their disregard of the biblical account, by [[John Arbuthnot]], [[John Edwards (divine)|John Edwards]] and [[William Nicolson]] in particular.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Stephen Gaukroger|author-link=Stephen Gaukroger|author2=John Schuster|author3=John Sutton|title=Descartes' Natural Philosophy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lguESFLTOl0C&pg=PA176|access-date=23 May 2013|year=2002|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-203-46301-7|pages=176–77}}</ref>

The title for Whiston's Boyle lectures was ''The Accomplishment of Scripture Prophecies''. Rejecting [[typology (theology)|typological]] interpretation of biblical prophecy, he argued that the meaning of a prophecy must be unique. His views were later challenged by [[Anthony Collins (philosopher)|Anthony Collins]].<ref>{{cite book|editor=Henk J. M. Nellen|author3=Edwin Rabbie|title=Hugo Grotius, Theologian: Essays in Honour of G. H. M. Posthumus Meyjes|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nULvj0SoH6sC&pg=PA195|access-date=22 May 2013|year=1994|publisher=Brill|isbn=978-90-04-10000-8|page=195}}</ref> There was a more immediate attack by [[Nicholas Clagett the younger|Nicholas Clagett]] in 1710.<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Clagett, Nicholas (1654-1727)|display=Clagett, Nicholas (1654–1727)|volume=10}}</ref> One reason prophecy was topical was the [[Camisard]] movement that saw French exiles ("French prophets") in England. Whiston had started writing on the [[millenarianism]] that was integral to the Newtonian theology, and wanted to distance his views from theirs, and in particular from those of [[John Lacy (merchant)|John Lacy]].<ref name="BF">{{cite book|author1=Jed Zachary Buchwald|author2=Mordechai Feingold|title=Newton and the origin of civilization|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wmFGvVvwon0C&pg=PA336|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2012|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-15478-7|page=336}}</ref> Meeting the French prophets in 1713, Whiston developed the view that the [[charismatic gift]] of revelation could be [[demonic possession]].{{sfn|Force|Hutton|2004|p=179|loc=note 102}}

===Tensions with Newton===
It is no longer assumed that Whiston's ''Memoirs'' are completely trustworthy on the matter of his personal relations with Newton. One view is that the relationship was never very close, Bentley being more involved in Whiston's appointment to the Lucasian chair; and that it deteriorated as soon as Whiston began to write on prophecy, publishing ''Essay on the Revelation of St John'' (1706).<ref name="BF"/> This work proclaimed the millennium for the year 1716.<ref>{{cite book |last=Jacob |first=Margaret C. |title=The Newtonians and the English Revolution 1689–1720 |year=1976 |publisher=Harvester Press |pages=132–33}}</ref>

Whiston's 1707 edition of Newton's ''[[Arithmetica Universalis]]'' did nothing to improve matters. Newton himself was heavily if covertly involved in the 1722 edition, nominally due to [[John Machin]], making many changes.<ref>{{cite book|editor=D. T. Whiteside|title=The Mathematical Papers of Isaac Newton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sf5z2h93_wcC&pg=PA14|access-date=22 May 2013|date=2008|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-04584-1|page=14}}</ref>

In 1708–9 Whiston was engaging [[Thomas Tenison]] and [[John Sharp (bishop)|John Sharp]] as archbishops in debates on the Trinity. There is evidence from [[Hopton Haynes]] that Newton reacted by pulling back from publication on the issue;{{sfn|Force|Hutton|2004|p=109}} his [[antitrinitarian]] views, from the 1690s, were finally published in 1754 as ''[[An Historical Account of Two Notable Corruptions of Scripture]]''.

Whiston was never a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]]. In conversation with [[Edmond Halley]] he blamed his reputation as a "heretick". Also, though, he claimed Newton had disliked having an independent-minded disciple; and was unnaturally cautious and suspicious by nature.<ref>{{cite book |editor=Richard H. Popkin |editor-link=Richard H. Popkin |title=The Pimlico History of Western Philosophy |year=1999 |publisher=Pimlico |isbn=0-7126-6534-X |page=427}}</ref>

==Unorthodox religious views==

===Expelled Arian===
Whiston's route to rejection of the [[Nicene Creed]], the historical orthodox position against [[Arianism]], began early in his tenure of the Lucasian chair as he followed hints from [[Samuel Clarke]]. He read also in [[Louis Ellies Dupin]], and the ''Explication of Gospel Theism'' (1706) of [[Richard Brocklesby (clergyman)|Richard Brocklesby]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Wiles |first=Maurice |author-link=Maurice Wiles|title=Archetypal Heresy: Arianism Through the Centuries|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gKWjIQtq5gQC&pg=PA94|access-date=22 May 2013|year=1996|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-826927-4|pages=94–}}</ref> His study of the ''[[Apostolic Constitutions]]'' then convinced him that Arianism was the creed of the early church.<ref name="EB1911"/>

The [[1710 British general election|general election of 1710]] brought the [[Tories (British political party)|Tories]] solid political power for a number of years, up to the [[Hanoverian succession]] of 1714. Their distrust of theological innovation had a direct impact on Whiston, as well as others of similar views. His [[heterodoxy]] was notorious.{{sfn|Gibson|2004|pp=121–123}} In 1710 he was deprived of his professorship and expelled from the university.<ref name="EB1911"/>

The matter was not allowed to rest there: Whiston tried to get a hearing before [[Convocation of the English Clergy|Convocation]]. He did have defenders even in the [[high church]] ranks, such as [[George Smalridge]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=William Gibson|author2=Robert G.. Ingram|title=Religious Identities in Britain: 1660– 1832|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gX5Mc_5snlcC&pg=PA47|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2005|publisher=Ashgate Publishing, Ltd.|isbn=978-0-7546-3209-2|pages=47–48}}</ref> For political reasons, this development would have been divisive at the time. [[Anne, Queen of Great Britain|Queen Anne]] made a point of twice "losing" the papers in the case.<ref>{{cite book|author1=William Gibson|author2=William Gibson|title=The Church of England 1688–1832: Unity and Accord|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qyel0pA36JgC&pg=PA81|access-date=22 May 2013|date=2002|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-203-13462-7|page=81}}</ref> After her death in 1714 the intended hearing was allowed to drop.<ref name="DNB">{{cite DNB|wstitle=Whiston, William|display=Whiston, William|volume=61}}</ref> The party passions of these years found an echo in [[Henry Sacheverell]]'s attempt to exclude Whiston from his church of [[St Andrew's, Holborn]], taking place in 1719.<ref name="DNB"/><ref>{{cite book |last=Steele |first=John M. |title=Ancient Astronomical Observations and the Study of the Moon's Motion (1691–1757)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rAuWlfyMGLkC&pg=PA24|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2012|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4614-2149-8|page=24}}</ref>

==="Primitive Christianity" and other religious scholarship===
[[File:William Whiston.png|thumb|right|Portrait of Whiston, early 18th century]]

Whiston founded a society for promoting primitive Christianity, lecturing in support of his theories in halls and [[coffee house|coffee-houses]] at London, [[Bath, Somerset|Bath]], and [[Tunbridge Wells]].<ref name="EB1911"/> Those he involved included [[Thomas Chubb]],<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=5378|title=Chubb, Thomas|first=Clive|last=Probyn}}</ref> [[Thomas Emlyn]],<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=8793|title=Emlyn, Thomas|first=H. J.|last=McLachlan}}</ref> [[John Gale (theologian)|John Gale]],<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=10292|title=Gale, John|first=Jim|last=Benedict}}</ref> [[Benjamin Hoadley]],{{sfn|Force|2002|p=27}} [[Arthur Onslow]],{{sfn|Force|2002}} and [[Thomas Rundle]].<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=24279|title=Rundle, Thomas|first=Alan R.|last=Acheson}}</ref> There were meetings at Whiston's house from 1715 to 1717; Hoadley avoided coming, as did Samuel Clarke, though invited.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sheehan |first=Jonathan |title="The" Enlightenment Bible: Translation, Scholarship, Culture|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SJGhYCqVflUC&pg=PA35|access-date=22 May 2013|year=2005|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-11887-1|page=35 note 21}}</ref> A meeting with Clarke, Hoadley, [[John Craig (mathematician)|John Craig]] and Gilbert Burnet the younger had left these leading [[latitudinarian]]s unconvinced about Whiston's reliance on the ''Apostolical Constitutions''.{{sfn|Gibson|2004|p=122}}

{{ill|Franz Woken|de||fr||pl}} wrote a 1728 Latin work on Whiston's view of primitive Christianity.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wokenius |first=Franz |title=Christianismus primaevus quem Guil. Whistonus modo non-probando restituendum dictitat sed Apostolus Paulus breviter quasi in tabula depinxit ...|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pVfitgAACAAJ|access-date=25 May 2013|year=1728}}</ref> His challenge to the teachings of [[Athanasius]] meant that Whiston was commonly considered [[heresy|heretical]] on many points. On the other hand, he was a firm believer in supernatural aspects of Christianity. He defended prophecy and miracle. He supported [[anoint]]ing the sick and touching for the [[king's evil]]. His dislike of [[rationalism]] in religion also made him one of the numerous opponents of Hoadley's ''Plain Account of the Nature and End of the Sacrament''. He was fervent in his views of ecclesiastical government and discipline, derived from the ''Apostolical Constitutions''.<ref name="EB1911"/>

Around 1747, when his clergyman began to read the [[Athanasian Creed]], which Whiston did not believe in, he physically left the church and the [[Anglican communion]], becoming a [[Baptist]].<ref name="EB1911"/>

By the 1720s, some [[dissenter]]s and early [[Unitarianism|Unitarians]] viewed Whiston as a role model.<ref name="ODNB Whiston"/>
The series of [[Moyer Lectures]] often made Whiston's unorthodox views a particular target.{{sfn|Force|Hutton|2004|p=102}}

Whiston held that ''[[Song of Solomon]]'' was [[apocrypha]]l and that the ''[[Book of Baruch]]'' was not.<ref name="EB1911"/> He modified the biblical [[Ussher chronology]], setting the [[Genesis creation narrative|Creation]] at 4010&nbsp;BCE.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Davis A. Young|author2=Ralph Stearley|title=The Bible, Rocks and Time: Geological Evidence for the Age of the Earth|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TRKtFWlSrRsC&pg=PA67|access-date=23 May 2013|date=2008|publisher=InterVarsity Press|isbn=978-0-8308-2876-0|page=67}}</ref> He challenged Newton's system of ''[[The Chronology of Ancient Kingdoms Amended]]'' (1728). Westfall absolves Whiston of the charge that he pushed for the posthumous publication of the ''Chronology'' just to attack it, commenting that the heirs were in any case looking to publish manuscripts of Newton, who died in 1727.<ref>{{cite book|last=Westfall |first=Richard S. |author-link=Richard S. Westfall|title=Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ngEugMMa9YC&pg=PA815|access-date=25 May 2013|date=1983|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-27435-7|pages=815 note 112}}</ref>

Whiston's advocacy of clerical [[monogamy]] is referenced in [[Oliver Goldsmith]]'s novel ''[[The Vicar of Wakefield]]''. His last "famous discovery, or rather revival of Dr [[Giles Fletcher, the Elder]]'s," which he mentions in his autobiography, was the identification of the [[Tatars]] with the [[lost tribes of Israel]].<ref name="EB1911"/>

==Scientific lecturer and popular author==
[[File:Whiston Senex solar system chart.jpg|thumb|upright=1.45|right|Solar System chart by William Whiston and [[John Senex]]]]

Whiston began lecturing on natural philosophy in London. He gave regular courses at [[coffee house#coffee in Europe|coffee house]]s, particularly Button's, and also at the Censorium, a set of riverside meeting rooms in London run by [[Richard Steele]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=Margaret C. Jacob|author2=Larry Stewart|title=Practical Matter: Newton's Science in the Service of Industry and Empire 1687–1851|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yU8zZrK2JPgC&pg=PA64|access-date=21 May 2013|year=2009|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-03903-2|page=64}}</ref> At Button's, he gave courses of demonstration lectures on astronomical and physical phenomena, and [[Francis Hauksbee the younger]] worked with him on experimental demonstrations. His passing remarks on religious topics were sometimes objected to, for example by [[Henry Newman (SPCK)|Henry Newman]] of the [[SPCK]] writing to Steele.<ref>{{MacTutor|title=London Coffee houses and mathematics|id=Coffee_houses|class=HistTopics}}</ref><ref>{{cite ODNB|id=12619|title=Hauksbee, Francis|first=Larry|last=Stewart}}</ref>

His lectures were often accompanied by publications. In 1712, he published, with [[John Senex]], a chart of the [[Solar System]] showing numerous paths of comets.<ref>{{cite book|editor1=Thomas Hockey|editor2=Katherine Bracher|editor3=Marvin Bolt|editor4=Virginia Trimble|editor5= Richard Jarrell|editor6=  JoAnn Palmeri|editor7=  Jordan D. Marché|editor8=  Thomas Williams|editor9=  F. Jamil Ragep|title=Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t-BF1CHkc50C&pg=PA1213|access-date=25 May 2013|year=2007|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-30400-7|page=1213}}</ref> In 1715, he lectured on the total [[solar eclipse of May 3, 1715|solar eclipse of 3 May 1715]] (which fell in April [[Old Style]] in England); Whiston lectured on it at the time, in [[Covent Garden]], and later, as a natural event and as a portent.{{sfn|Knox|2003|p=162}}

By 1715 Whiston had also become adept at newspaper advertising.<ref name="Wigelsworth2010">{{cite book |last=Wigelsworth |first=Jeffrey R. |title=Selling Science in the Age of Newton: Advertising and the Commoditization of Knowledge|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Yi2S_ZiFxaQC&pg=PA137|access-date=25 May 2013|year=2010|publisher=Ashgate Publishing, Ltd.|isbn=978-1-4094-2310-2|page=137}}</ref> He frequently lectured to the Royal Society.

===Longitude===
In 1714, he was instrumental in the passing of the [[Longitude Act]], which established the [[Board of Longitude]]. In collaboration with [[Humphrey Ditton]] he published ''A New Method for Discovering the Longitude, both at Sea and Land'',<ref name="WhistonDitton1714">{{cite book |last1=Ditton |first1=William Whiston |last2=Ditton |first2=Humphrey |title=A New Method for Discovering the Longitude, both at Sea and Land|url=https://writersinspire.podcasts.ox.ac.uk/content/new-method-discovering-longitude-both-sea-land-humbly-proposed-consideration-publick-william|access-date=15 April 2015|year=1714|publisher=John Phillips}}</ref> which was widely referenced and discussed. For the next forty years he continued to propose a range of methods to solve the [[Longitude prize|longitude reward]], which earned him widespread ridicule, particularly from the group of writers known as the [[Scriblerians]].<ref>For example, [[Jonathan Swift]]'s 1714 [https://archive.org/details/miscellaniesinf00gaygoog/page/n154/mode/2up?view=theater "Ode, to Musick. On the Longitude"], including numerous references to bepissing and beshitting upon both Whiston and Ditton.</ref><ref>S.D. Snobelen, "William Whiston: Natural Philosopher, Prophet, Primitive Christian" (Cambridge Univ. PhD Thesis, 2000)</ref> In one proposal for using magnetic dip to find longitude he produced one of the first [[Isoclinic line|isoclinic]] maps of southern England in 1719 and 1721. In 1734, he proposed using the [[eclipse]]s of [[Moons of Jupiter|Jupiter's satellites]].<ref>[http://cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/view/MS-MSS-00079-00130-00002/1 Mr Whiston's Project for finding the Longitude (MSS/79/130.2)], Board of Longitude project, [[University of Cambridge]] Digital Library</ref>

===Broader natural philosophy===
[[File:WilliamWhistonComet.jpg|thumb|right|A portrait of William Whiston with a diagram demonstrating his theories of cometary catastrophism, described in ''[[A New Theory of the Earth]]'']]

Whiston's ''[[A New Theory of the Earth|A New Theory of the Earth from its Original to the Consummation of All Things]]'' (1696) was an articulation of [[creationism]] and [[flood geology]]. It held that the [[deluge (mythology)|global flood]] of [[Noah]] had been caused by a [[comet]]. The work obtained the praise of [[John Locke]], who classed the author among those who, if not adding much to our knowledge, "At least bring some new things to our thoughts."<ref name="EB1911"/> He was an early advocate, along with [[Edmond Halley]], of the periodicity of comets; he also held that comets were responsible for past [[catastrophism|catastrophes]] in Earth's history. In 1736, he caused widespread anxiety among London's citizens when he predicted the world would end on [[October 16|16 October]] that year because a comet would hit the earth.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201511/physicshistory.cfm|title=This Month in Physics History|language=en|access-date=2018-10-16}}</ref> [[William Wake]] as [[Archbishop of Canterbury]] officially denied this prediction to calm the public.

There was no consensus within the Newtonians as to how far mechanical causes could be held responsible for key events of sacred history: [[John Keill]] was at the opposite extreme to Whiston in minimising such causes.{{sfn|Poole|2010|p=72}} As a natural philosopher, Whiston's speculations respected no boundary with his theological views. He saw the creation of man as an intervention in the [[Natural order (philosophy)|natural order]]. He picked up on [[Arthur Ashley Sykes]]'s advice to Samuel Clarke to omit an eclipse and earthquake mentioned by [[Phlegon of Tralles]] from future editions of Clarke's Boyle lectures, these events being possibly synchronous with [[Christ's crucifixion]]. Whiston published ''The Testimony of Phlegon Vindicated'' in 1732.<ref name="Force1985">{{cite book |last=Force |first=James E. |title=William Whiston: Honest Newtonian|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=np9s8TGaSnYC&pg=PA181|access-date=25 May 2013|year=1985|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-26590-4|page=181 note 128}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Whiston married Ruth, daughter of George Antrobus, his headmaster at Tamworth school. He died in [[Lyndon, Rutland|Lyndon]] Hall, [[Rutland]], at the home of his son-in-law, [[Samuel Barker (Hebraist)|Samuel Barker]], on 22 August 1752.<ref name="ODNB Whiston"/> He was survived by his children Sarah, William, George, and John.{{sfn|Farrell|1981|pp=46–47}}

==Works==
[[File:Whiston, William – New theory of the Earth, 1696 – BEIC 4762925.jpg|thumb|''New theory of the Earth'', 1696]]

Whiston's later life was spent in continual controversy: [[theology|theological]], mathematical, [[chronology|chronological]], and miscellaneous. He vindicated his estimate of the ''Apostolical Constitutions'' and the Arian views he had derived from them in his ''Primitive Christianity Revived'' (5 vols., 1711–1712). In 1713 he produced a reformed [[liturgy]]. His ''Life of Samuel Clarke'' appeared in 1730.<ref name="EB1911"/>

In 1727 he published a two volume work called ''Authentik Record belonging to the Old and New Testament''. This was a collection of translations and essays on various deuterocanonical books, pseudepigrapha and other essays with a translation if relevant.<ref name="EB1911"/>

Whiston translated the complete works of [[Josephus]] into English, and published them along with his own notes and dissertations under the title ''The Genuine Works of Flavius Josephus the Jewish Historian'' in 1737. This translation was based on the same Greek edition of Josephus' works used by [[Siwart Haverkamp]] in his prior translation.<ref>{{cite web |title=The genuine works of Flavius Josephus the Jewish historian |url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/josephus/ |publisher=University of Chicago |access-date=16 June 2023}}</ref> The text on which Whiston's translation of Josephus is based is, reputedly, one which had many errors in transcription.<ref>{{cite book |last=Josephus |author-link=Josephus |title=Josephus Complete Works |publisher=Kregel Publications |translator=William Whiston |date=1981|location=Grand Rapids, Michigan |page= xi (Foreword)|language=en|isbn=0-8254-2951-X }}</ref> In 1745 he published his ''Primitive New Testament'' (on the basis of [[Codex Bezae]] and [[Codex Claromontanus]]).<ref>{{cite book | last = Alexander | first = Philip | editor1-last = Khan | editor1-first = Geoffrey | editor2-last = Lipton | editor2-first = Diana | contribution = Reflections on the Christian Turn to the Hebraica Veritas and Its Implications | date = January 2012 | doi = 10.1163/9789004217379_027 | isbn = 9789004217300 | pages = 353–372 | publisher = BRILL | series = Vetus Testamentum, Supplements | title = Studies on the Text and Versions of the Hebrew Bible in Honour of Robert Gordon | volume = 149}}</ref>

Whiston left memoirs (3 vols., 1749–1750). These do not contain the account of the proceedings taken against him at Cambridge for his [[antitrinitarianism]], which was published separately at the time.<ref name="EB1911"/>
